# WhatsApp AI Agent That Sells & Understands Every Customer | plumcut

Source: https://plumcut.com/
Updated: 2026-10-06

Beyond the reply

## Automate your business. Know every customer.

Chat with plum
See how it works →
Every business runs on the same repetitive tasks and conversations. We build automation that handles all of it… automation that answers like a human, sells like a pro, and never sleeps. And while it works, it listens, so every conversation becomes insight into what your customers actually want.
The problem

### Two things are quietly costing you

#### The sales you can see slipping

A reply that comes six hours late is a sale you never see. Conversion drops sharply within minutes, and your customers message at midnight, when no one's there to answer. The ready-to-buy ones don't wait. They move on.

#### The customers you can't see

Every WhatsApp conversation is full of signals, what they want, what they hesitate on, what they keep asking for that you don't even sell. It disappears, because no one can read thousands of conversations. So you guess at what to stock, and why people buy.
How plum sells

### From "is this available?" to a confirmed order

#### Answers instantly, in your voice

Availability, shipping, returns, the same question for the hundredth time, answered in seconds, the way you'd answer it.

#### Sells, doesn't just reply

Recommends the right product, suggests the matching add-on, nudges the hesitant buyer, and recovers the cart before it's gone.

#### Books and closes

From "do you have this?" to a confirmed order or appointment, without you touching a single message.
The insight layer

### plum sells to them, then tells you about them

Because plum is in every conversation, it sees what no dashboard can: why people buy, why they don't, the things they keep asking for, the demand you can't even see. You get a clear picture that turns thousands of chats into decisions, and it's yours. Your data, your customers, not locked inside a platform.
What plum does

### Solutions that work together

From the first "hello" to the final receipt: not a stack of separate tools, but one connected layer that answers, sells, books, and learns from every conversation.

#### Instant answers

Availability, shipping, returns, product questions, answered in seconds, in your voice, day and night. The same question for the hundredth time, handled, so you never lose a buyer to silence.

#### Order tracking

"Where's my package?" handled end to end. plum confirms orders, sends updates, and tracks shipments, so those messages stop landing on you and your customers stay calm.

#### Smart selling

The part most bots skip. plum recommends the right product, suggests the matching add-on, nudges the hesitant buyer, and rescues the cart before it goes cold, closing in the conversation.

#### Bookings & orders

Fill your calendar while you sleep. Customers pick a slot or place an order, get instant confirmation, and receive reminders, appointments and orders closed without a single back-and-forth from you.

#### In-chat payments

Close and collect in the same conversation. plum sends a secure payment link the moment a customer's ready, confirms it instantly, and never leaves money waiting on a follow-up.

#### Customer insights

The dashboard you own. Because plum is in every chat, it shows you why people buy, what they keep asking for, and what to stock next, decisions, not just metrics. Your data, your customers.

How it works

## plum does the talking, & we do everything else.

You don't set anything up, learn any software, or manage a single conversation. We build plum around your brand, launch it on WhatsApp, and run it for you, so all you do is watch the sales and the insight come in.

### From first hello to selling on its own, in three steps

01

#### We learn your brand

We sit down with you once and learn how you talk, what you sell, your policies, your prices, and the questions you get asked a hundred times a week. That's the only real time you'll spend. Everything plum says afterward sounds like you, not a robot.
02

We build plum around what we learned and connect it to the channels your customers already use, WhatsApp and your store. In about two weeks plum is live on WhatsApp, answering, selling, and booking. You don't touch a tool, write a flow, or configure anything.
03

#### We run, sell & improve

plum keeps working day and night. We watch it, fix what needs fixing, and sharpen how it sells as it learns your customers, week after week. You get the results, and a clear picture of what your customers actually want. It gets better the longer it runs.

Customer understanding

### why they buy, and why they don't.

Automating your chats won't disconnect you from your customers. You'll understand them better and faster than before.

#### who is ready to buy

the leads most likely to convert, ranked so you call them first.

#### lead temperature

how warm each lead is right now: hot, warm, or cold.

#### hot leads

the contacts showing the strongest intent to buy today.

#### qualified leads

people who fit your offer and gave enough buying info.

#### what they keep asking for

the questions your customers raise again and again.

#### why they didn't book

the real reasons people stopped short of booking.

#### conversion funnel

how many move from first chat to confirmed booking.

#### sentiment

how customers feel in their chats: positive, neutral, or negative.

#### booking conversion

the share of chats that turn into real bookings.

#### preferred booking day

the days customers most often ask to be booked.

#### sentiment trajectory

whether a conversation is warming up or cooling down.

#### objection raised

the doubts and pushbacks customers bring up before buying.

#### how objections were handled

whether the bot resolved each objection or left it open.

#### buying signals

the words and moments that show someone's ready to buy.

#### urgency level

how soon a customer wants to move, from now to later.

#### preferred booking time

the times of day customers most want to book.

#### where conversation drop off

the exact points where chats stall and people leave.

#### top pain points

the problems customers complain about most, in their words.

#### budget posture

what customers signal they're willing to spend.

#### risk and safety flags

anything sensitive that needs a human to step in.

#### tools they already used

the competing tools and brands your customers mention.

#### feature demand

the features and products customers ask for most.

#### languages used

the languages your customers actually chat in.

#### priority queue

your leads sorted by who to follow up with first.

#### recommended action

the next best move per lead: call, nurture, or close.

#### Order tracking

06

#### Gets paid in chat

FAQ

### More details about the pricing

How much does plum cost?
Two parts. A one-time setup fee for the build, then a fixed monthly fee to run it. The
monthly fee is set by how much your solution does, not by how many conversations it
handles. Meta messaging and AI usage are billed to you at cost, with nothing added
by us. Tell plum about your brand and we'll put a real number in front of you on a
15-minute call.
Do I have to operate anything?
No. plumcut is done for you. We learn your brand, build plum, connect your
channels, and run and improve it day to day, see exactly
how it works.
You read the results, you never touch a tool, write a flow, or manage a single
conversation.
How fast until plum is live?
About two weeks from our first conversation. We learn your brand, build and test
plum on real questions, you sign off, and it goes live on WhatsApp, answering,
selling, and booking. From there we keep tuning it so it gets sharper every week.
Is there a setup fee?
Yes, one payment at the start, and we're upfront about it. It pays for learning your
brand and building and launching plum around your voice, products, and policies. After
that you're on a fixed monthly fee.
Do I own my data?
Yes. Everything plum learns about your customers, the conversations, the
patterns, the understanding of why they buy, why they don't, and everything they keep asking for, belongs to you.
It isn't locked inside a platform you'd lose if you left. Your brand, your
customers, your data.
What if my message volume suddenly spikes?
Nothing changes. Your monthly fee covers a wide band of traffic, so a busy month sits
inside it. If your traffic settles at a higher level, the fee steps up one band, and we
tell you before it does.
How does your pricing model work?
A one-time setup fee for the build, then a fixed monthly fee to run and maintain it. The
monthly fee is set by how much your solution does, and it steps up in wide bands as your
traffic grows, up to a ceiling. Meta messaging and AI usage are billed to you at
cost, with no margin from us.
Can I start with one solution and add more later?
Yes. Start with what you need most, answering, selling, booking, and add
solutions,
like the customer-insights dashboard, as you grow. Adding one changes your monthly
fee, and you see the new figure before you agree to it.
Does my fee change as I grow?
It steps up in wide bands, and each band covers a broad range of traffic, so most growth
costs you nothing. The top band is a ceiling, so there is no figure above it. We always
tell you before a band changes.

# Privacy Policy | plumcut

Source: https://plumcut.com/privacy
Updated: 2026-10-06

## Privacy

### What happens to your information when you talk to plum.

Last updated 4 September 2026
plum is our AI sales agent on WhatsApp. When you message her, real information about you passes through our systems. This page says plainly what we keep, why we keep it, who else sees it, and how to make us delete it. No legal fog.

#### Who we are

plumcut is a small team based in Beirut, Lebanon. We build and run AI sales agents for WhatsApp. We decide what happens to the information described here, which makes us responsible for it.
Anything on this page, write to info@plumcut.com.

#### What we collect

Only what arrives in a conversation you start. We do not buy lists and we do not scrape anyone.
Your WhatsApp number and the profile name you have set
What you send - text, images, voice notes, documents
Anything you volunteer - your name, email, company, what you are after
Booking details when you ask plum for a meeting
Do not send card numbers, passwords or ID documents. If you do, we delete them.

#### Why we use it

To answer you, to book the meetings you ask for, and to remember the conversation so you do not have to repeat yourself next time. In aggregate, we look at what customers ask about so plum gets better at answering.
We do not sell your data. We do not use your conversation to send you unrelated marketing.

#### plum is an AI

Your messages are processed by a language model to generate replies. That is automated, but nothing plum does makes a legal or similarly significant decision about you - she answers, informs and books.
You can always reach a person. Ask plum for a human, or email info@plumcut.com, and one of us takes over.

#### How long we keep it

Conversation records are kept for 24 months after your last message, then deleted. Booking records last as long as the meeting and our own bookkeeping need them. Ask us sooner and we delete sooner.

#### Your rights

You can ask us for a copy of what we hold, have it corrected, have it deleted, or tell us to stop using it. Email info@plumcut.com and we answer within 30 days. Or just message plum and ask to be deleted - that works too.

#### Security and children

Messages are encrypted in transit by WhatsApp. Our systems are access-controlled and limited to the people who need them. No system is perfect, so do not send us anything you would not want stored.
plum is for adults doing business. We do not knowingly collect data from anyone under 18 - tell us if that happens and we delete it.

#### Changes

If this policy changes, the date at the top changes with it. Anything material gets announced on the site.
plumcut
Beirut, Lebanon
info@plumcut.com

# Click to WhatsApp Ads: What Happens After the Click

Source: https://plumcut.com/blog/click-to-whatsapp-ads-after-the-click
Published: 2026-10-17

A click to WhatsApp ad does one job: it opens a chat. Everything that decides whether you make money happens after that, inside a conversation most brands never look at. When a business tells us its WhatsApp ads "don't convert", the ad is rarely the problem. The chat is.

This guide covers what happens between the tap and the sale, what Meta changed in its pricing in late 2026, and which parts of the conversation are worth automating.

## The click is not the lead

Ads Manager reports "messaging conversations started". That number counts people who tapped and sent a first message, often the prefilled "Hi, I want to know more". It does not count people who got an answer, people who asked a price and left, or people who bought.

Between the click and the sale there are four places a customer drops:

**The first reply.** The customer writes at 11:40 at night after seeing your ad. If the first answer comes the next morning, the intent is gone. They have already messaged two competitors who were faster.

**The first real question.** Most ad chats open with a price, a size, a branch or a delivery area. A greeting followed by "how can I help?" adds a turn and loses people. The answer has to be the reply.

**The moment of choice.** The customer is interested but undecided. This is where a helpful suggestion (the bundle, the larger size, the booking slot tonight) turns interest into an order.

**The follow up.** Many people say "I'll think about it". Whether anyone comes back to them decides a large share of the sales the ad paid for.

If you only measure cost per conversation, you can't see any of this. A campaign with cheaper chats can sell less than one with expensive chats that get answered properly.

## What Meta changed in 2026

[Two pricing changes](/blog/whatsapp-business-api-cost) make the post-click conversation more important than it was a year ago.

**Service replies now cost money.** From 1 October 2026, Meta charges per message for service messages, the normal free-form replies your team or AI sends inside the 24-hour window. Each business number gets 1,000 free service messages a month, and after that every reply is billed. Utility templates sent in reply to a customer are also charged again. In practice, long conversations with many short replies now cost more than short conversations that answer in one complete message.

**The free entry point window is the exception.** When a customer messages you from a click to WhatsApp ad on the WhatsApp mobile app, and you reply within 24 hours, Meta opens a free entry point window from the moment you reply. Inside it, marketing, utility, authentication and service messages are not charged. Meta's pricing documentation now says this window can stay open for "up to 7 days". Earlier documentation and many providers still describe it as 72 hours. Either way, three conditions decide whether you get it:

- The chat must start on the WhatsApp Android or iOS app. Desktop and web do not open the window.
- You must reply inside the first 24 hours. No reply, no free window.
- Meta Business Agent messages are still charged by token inside the window. Third party AI replies are not charged by Meta inside it, though your provider may charge for them.

So the conversations your ads bring in are now the cheapest conversations you'll ever have with a customer, but only if someone answers quickly.

## What a good post-click conversation looks like

Take a supermarket running a Ramadan basket ad in Beirut, or a fashion brand in Dubai promoting a new collection. A strong ad conversation usually has five parts.

**An instant first answer that matches the ad.** If the ad promoted a basket, the first reply talks about the basket: what is in it, the price, delivery areas. The customer should never have to repeat what they just saw.

**One complete answer per question.** Price, stock, branch, delivery time and payment options in one message, not spread across four. With service messages now billed, fewer turns mean a lower bill and a faster customer.

**A relevant offer at the decision point.** Not a catalogue dump. One suggestion that belongs in the basket or the booking, offered once.

**A clean handover.** When the customer asks for something only a person can do, a staff member takes over with the full context, not a fresh "how can I help?".

**A follow up inside the free window.** A reminder on day two or three, while it still costs nothing, recovers a share of the "I'll think about it" customers who would otherwise vanish.

## What to automate and what to keep human

Automation pays most where volume is high and the answer is known:

- First replies at any hour, in Arabic, English or the [Arabizi mix customers actually write in](/blog/ai-customer-service-arabic)
- Prices, stock, sizes, branches, opening hours and delivery areas
- Building the order or booking and sending it to your system
- Follow ups and reminders inside the free entry point window

Keep a person on:

- Complaints and refunds
- Custom or high-value orders
- Anything where the customer asks for a human

The aim is not to remove your team from ad conversations. It is to make sure no paid conversation waits overnight, and that your team spends its time on the chats where a human closes the sale.

## Measure the conversation, not just the ad

Track these alongside your Ads Manager numbers:

- **Time to first reply** for ad conversations, by hour of day
- **Share of ad chats that got a complete answer** to their first question
- **Orders or bookings per 100 ad conversations**
- **Share of follow ups sent inside the free window**
- **What people asked that you couldn't answer** (often a product you don't stock or a delivery area you don't cover)

The last one is the most underrated. Ad conversations are customer research you've already paid for. Read across them and they tell you what your market wants, which objections kill the sale, and which promotions bring buyers rather than browsers.

## The bottom line

If your click to WhatsApp ads are not converting, look at the chat before you change the creative. Answer instantly, answer completely, make one relevant offer, follow up while it is free, and read what customers are telling you. That is where the budget is won or lost.

plumcut builds and runs an [intelligent automation system](/solutions) on the channels your customers already use. It answers, sells and books, and shows you what customers actually want. If you run ads that open WhatsApp and want to see what happens after the click, talk to us.

## Sources

Pricing rules checked on 17 October 2026. Meta changes them on a schedule, so confirm the current terms before you budget.

- Meta for Developers, [Pricing on the WhatsApp Business Platform](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/business-messaging/whatsapp/pricing): service message charges from 1 October 2026, the 1,000 free service messages per business phone number each month, utility templates charged inside the customer service window, and the free entry point window for click to WhatsApp ads.
- Meta for Developers, [Upcoming pricing updates for Meta Business Agent, service and utility messages](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/business-messaging/whatsapp/pricing/non-template-messages): Meta Business Agent messages billed by token and not covered by the free entry point window.

# WhatsApp Conversation Analysis: What Your Chats Reveal

Source: https://plumcut.com/blog/whatsapp-conversation-analysis
Published: 2026-10-14

WhatsApp conversation analysis tells you what customers ask most, what they want that you do not sell, why they hesitate, and when they message, using chats you already have.

For a lot of brands in Lebanon and the Gulf, WhatsApp is where the selling actually happens. Months of it sit in the phone: every "do you have this in black", every "how much is delivery to Jbeil", every customer who asked a price and went quiet. It is the best customer research the business owns, and most businesses never read it.

> WhatsApp conversation analysis means reading your chat history as research. Export the chats, define what one conversation is, separate staff from customers, then count the patterns and also read samples by hand, because counting alone misses most of the real reasons people message. Classify every conversation against one fixed list, measure twice, and treat voice notes and screenshots as a known gap. The output is a short list of decisions: what to stock, what to answer once in writing, what to offer, and when to staff the inbox.

## What an owner should get out of it

An analysis is only worth doing if it ends in decisions. These are the six outputs that do.

| What the chats show | The decision it feeds |
| --- | --- |
| The questions customers ask most, grouped by product or item | Product pages, a written FAQ, and the answers an assistant should give |
| What customers ask for that you do not sell | Stock and range: the sizes, colours, items or areas you keep turning away |
| Objections, and why people did not buy | Price, delivery fees, payment options, offers |
| Sentiment and motivation | What to lead with in ads and replies |
| Peak times | When the inbox needs more people, and when it is quiet |
| The answers your team repeats every day | What to automate first |

That last row is the one most owners underestimate. If the same three answers are typed fifty times a week, that is the first job to hand to automation, and we wrote up how to choose in [what to automate first in an ecommerce business](/blog/what-to-automate-first-ecommerce).

## What we learned analysing 18 exported WhatsApp groups

This section is plumcut's own work. We analysed 18 exported WhatsApp groups for a regional delivery company, which stays anonymous here. Six lessons came out of it, and each one would have quietly ruined the result if we had missed it.

**Counting found a handful of reasons. Reading kept finding more.** Counting keyword patterns produced only a handful of reasons people message. Reading conversations by hand kept surfacing new ones in every batch of 50 we read. Patterns alone missed most of the real reasons, so the method has to be both: count to see the size of things, read to see what they are.

**A "conversation" has to be defined before you count one.** A WhatsApp group is one endless thread. We cut it into conversations wherever there were 24 hours of silence. That is a choice, not a fact: a 12 hour cut gives more, shorter conversations, and a 48 hour cut gives fewer, longer ones. Pick one, write it down, and keep it fixed, or two analyses of the same chats will disagree for no reason.

**Exports do not all look the same.** Some files used 12 hour time and some 24 hour, some had two digit years, and media appeared as a placeholder such as `<Media omitted>`. Our first parser silently read 7 of the 18 files as empty. Nothing crashed. The numbers just came out wrong. Check how many messages your parser read from every single file before you trust anything downstream.

**Tell staff from customers by behaviour, not by name.** Contact names in an export are whatever was saved on the phone. Behaviour is more reliable: staff acknowledge, confirm and appear across many chats; customers ask, and usually appear in one.

**Questions and follow-ups share the same thread.** Nearly half the threads mixed inbound requests from customers with outbound follow-ups from the team. You cannot analyse "questions" and "follow-ups" as two separate piles, because they are tangled in the same conversations.

**Voice notes and screenshots set a ceiling.** A real share of requests sat inside voice notes and screenshots that a text-only analysis cannot read. The voice notes were short, most under 15 seconds, spoken one-liners. In a region where customers send voice notes and mix English, Arabic and Arabizi in one message ("3andkon delivery la Saida?"), any text-only analysis has a ceiling. We covered how far language understanding has come in [whether AI customer service really works in Arabic](/blog/ai-customer-service-arabic).

## Why "count and read" beats either one alone

Counting is fast and gives you proportions. It also only finds what you already thought to search for. If you search for "price", "delivery" and "size", you will find price, delivery and size, and you will miss the customer who wanted to know whether the item fits in a car boot.

Reading is slow and finds the reasons nobody predicted. It also cannot tell you whether a reason is one customer or four hundred.

So the working method is a loop. Count with the reasons you have. Read a batch of 50 conversations by hand. Add any new reason to the list. Count again. Stop reading when a whole batch adds nothing new.

## Response time is part of what customers are buying

One logistics operator we spoke to had already run about a thousand of its customer chats through an AI model. Their finding: response time drives willingness to pay, while late cash settlements and silence on lost orders kill it. In a market where many orders are paid in cash on delivery, the settlement is part of the service, and the chats are where customers say so.

That is a useful reminder of what analysis is for. It is not a word cloud. It is finding the two or three things that decide whether customers stay, in their own words.

## How to analyse your WhatsApp conversations, step by step

1. **Export the chats.** In WhatsApp, open the chat, open the menu, choose More, then [Export chat](https://faq.whatsapp.com/1180414079177245/?cms_platform=android), and pick Without media or Include media. You get a text file. WhatsApp notes that chats with Advanced chat privacy turned on cannot be exported.
2. **Strip phone numbers first.** Remove numbers and names before the file goes into any tool, and check what that tool's provider keeps. Our guide to [customer data safety with an AI chatbot](/blog/ai-chatbot-customer-data-safety) lists the questions to ask.
3. **Set the conversation cut.** Choose a silence gap, such as 24 hours, and use it everywhere.
4. **Clean the formats.** Normalise dates, times and years. Count the messages read from each file, and treat any file with zero as a parser bug until proven otherwise.
5. **Label senders.** Mark staff and customers by behaviour: who acknowledges across many chats, and who asks in one.
6. **Count, then read.** Run the keyword counts, then read samples of 50 by hand until a batch adds no new reason.
7. **Use one fixed list of reasons.** Classify every conversation against the same list, so this month and next month can be compared.
8. **Measure twice.** Measure a second time, independently, with a different method, for example a person labelling a sample against an AI model labelling all of it, and compare. Where they disagree, read those conversations.
9. **Separate "fully handled" from "partly handled".** If you are sizing automation, split conversations that could be fully handled without a person from those that could be partly handled but still end with a person. Never present the partial number as automation.
10. **Treat media as a known gap.** Report the share of conversations containing voice notes or screenshots next to every result.
11. **Turn findings into decisions.** Stock, FAQ, offers, staffing. If a finding does not change one of those, it is trivia.

## Where plumcut fits

plumcut builds and runs plum on a brand's WhatsApp. plum answers customers, actively sells (upsell, cross-sell, booking), and reads across every interaction to show the owner what customers actually want.

The third part of that sentence is this post. A one-off export analysis is a snapshot. When the assistant is already in every conversation, the questions, objections, missing products and peak hours can be read as they happen, and you can see [how it works](/how-it-works) or [what it does for different kinds of business](/solutions).

## What to do this week

1. Export your three busiest WhatsApp chats or groups, without media.
2. Strip the phone numbers.
3. Read 50 conversations by hand and write down every reason someone messaged.
4. Circle the requests for things you do not sell, and the answers you typed more than once.
5. Pick one decision from that list and make it before the end of the week.

# AI Chatbot Wrong Answers: Who Catches Them and How Fast

Source: https://plumcut.com/blog/ai-chatbot-wrong-answers
Published: 2026-10-14

AI chatbot wrong answers happen with every assistant, so what matters is how fast you see one, who steps in, and whether the customer ever notices.

Every vendor demo shows the assistant getting it right. We run one on WhatsApp for brands in Lebanon and the region, so this is the other half: the ways it fails, one failure of our own, told plainly, and what we built so that a mistake costs a minute instead of a customer.

> AI chatbot wrong answers are inevitable, so judge an assistant by its recovery, not its demo. Ground it in the business's own catalogue and policies, and make it say "let me check with the team" instead of guessing. Let staff see every conversation live and take it over in the same WhatsApp thread, with a handback when they are done. Escalate anger, refunds, health and legal questions, and repeated questions to a person. And monitor for silence, because a reply that was written but never delivered is worse than a wrong one: nobody sees an error, and the customer just waits.

## The five ways an AI chatbot gets it wrong

"Wrong answer" covers more than a wrong fact. These are the five failures we design against.

| Failure | What the customer sees | How you catch it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Confident wrong answer | A wrong price, a wrong stock status, a policy that does not exist | Answer only from live catalogue and written policy; review flagged answers |
| Silent failure | Nothing. No reply at all | Compare replies generated with replies delivered; alert on any gap |
| Double reply | The assistant and a staff member both answer, sometimes differently | A takeover flag per conversation, re-checked right before sending |
| Wrong or missing escalation | Stuck with the assistant when they needed a person, or handed over for nothing | Clear escalation rules, plus a visible route to a person |
| Misread voice note or mixed message | An answer to a question they did not ask | Confirm before acting on anything unclear |

The last row matters more in this region than in most. Customers here send short voice notes and mix English, Arabic and Arabizi in one line, such as "3andkon hayda bl aswad?" ("do you have this in black?"). An assistant that misreads that should ask, not guess. We looked at how well this works today in [whether AI customer service really works in Arabic](/blog/ai-customer-service-arabic).

## Silence is worse than a wrong answer: our own incident

When we added the check that decides whether a human or the assistant should answer a conversation, one step in the workflow read the wrong field. A database lookup ran in between, and the step assumed the assistant's reply was still where it had been before that lookup. It was not, so the step erased the reply before it reached the customer.

For about ninety minutes, one customer sent six messages and got nothing back, although a reply had been written each time.

The fix was small: the step now names the exact source of its answer instead of assuming the field is still there. The lost replies and records were rebuilt from the workflow's own execution history, not guessed.

The lesson was bigger. A wrong answer is visible: the customer replies "that's not right", and someone sees it. Silence is invisible. The assistant thinks it answered, the dashboard looks calm, and the customer concludes nobody is there. So we now monitor for replies that were generated but never delivered, and treat any gap as an incident.

## How human takeover should work

Almost every business we speak to assumes its team can step into the chat at any moment. One wanted several staff accounts on the business number so anyone could jump in. That expectation is right, and the system should be built for it.

- **A per-conversation switch.** Each conversation has a flag, take over or return to assistant, shown on a dashboard. Flipping it affects that one customer, not the whole inbox.
- **One thread, one number.** The customer stays in the same WhatsApp thread with the same business number. They cannot tell who is replying, and they never have to start again.
- **Re-check before sending.** A takeover can land while the assistant is still writing. The assistant checks the flag again right before it sends, and drops its reply if a person has taken over.
- **Auto-release.** If the person goes quiet for about 15 minutes, the conversation returns to the assistant, so chats do not get stranded.
- **No false typing.** The assistant's typing indicator is suppressed during a takeover, so the customer is not shown activity that will not produce a reply.
- **One owner.** Decide which staff member owns a taken-over conversation, so two people do not answer the same customer at once.

This is also policy, not just good service. Meta's [WhatsApp Business Messaging Policy](https://whatsappbusiness.com/policy/) permits automated replies within the customer service window but requires businesses to offer prompt, clear and direct escalation paths to a person. We wrote up the rest of the handover design in [how to automate customer service without losing the customer](/blog/automate-customer-service-without-losing-customers).

## The 24 hour window decides what your team can send

Takeover has a clock on it. On the WhatsApp Business Platform, a customer's message opens a [24 hour customer service window](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/business-messaging/whatsapp/messages/send-messages), and each new message from them resets it. Inside the window, the business can send free-form replies. Outside it, only template messages can be sent, and templates generally need Meta's approval first.

So a dashboard should show how much of the window is left on every taken-over conversation, and offer an approved template once it expires. A staff member who picks up a chat 23 hours late needs to know they have one hour, not find out when the message fails.

On cost, checked on 14 October 2026: Meta's [pricing page](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/business-messaging/whatsapp/pricing) says that, from 1 October 2026, each business phone number gets 1,000 free service messages a month, and service messages are charged from the 1,001st. Unused free messages do not roll over. Confirm the current figures for your number before you budget, because Meta changes them on a schedule.

## Guardrails that stop most wrong answers

- **Answer only from the business's own catalogue and policies.** If it is not in the catalogue or the written policy, the assistant does not know it.
- **Say "let me check with the team" instead of guessing.** A short wait for a correct answer beats a fast wrong one.
- **Escalate by rule.** Anger, refund requests, health and legal topics, and the same question asked twice all go to a person.
- **Log everything.** Every conversation, every handover and every failure should be recorded so it can be replayed and fixed, not just apologised for.

## Questions to ask any AI chatbot vendor

1. What does it say when it does not know the answer?
2. Who gets notified when it hands over, and how?
3. Can we see every conversation live?
4. Can staff take over a single conversation and hand it back?
5. How are failures logged, and can you replay what happened?
6. How fast would you hear about a silent failure, a reply that was never delivered?

If a vendor answers the last one with "that doesn't happen", keep asking. It happened to us. For the data side of the same conversation, see [is customer data safe with an AI chatbot](/blog/ai-chatbot-customer-data-safety).

## Where plumcut fits

plumcut builds and runs plum, which answers, sells and books on a brand's WhatsApp, with the team able to step in on any conversation. The design above is the one we run, and the incident above is why the delivery monitoring exists. You can see [how it works](/how-it-works), and what the assistant learns from all those conversations is covered in [WhatsApp conversation analysis](/blog/whatsapp-conversation-analysis).

## What to do this week

1. Send your current assistant, or the one you are considering, five questions it should not be able to answer. Note which ones it guesses.
2. Ask your team how they would take over a conversation right now, and time it.
3. Check whether anyone would know if replies stopped being delivered for an hour.
4. Write down the four topics that must always go to a person, and make sure the assistant has them.

# WhatsApp Ordering for Supermarkets When You Already Have an App

Source: https://plumcut.com/blog/whatsapp-ordering-supermarkets
Published: 2026-10-06

WhatsApp ordering for supermarkets still pays when you already have an app, as a parallel channel for shoppers who will never install it, for ad traffic and for quick reorders.

If most of your customers already order through your app, a WhatsApp ordering channel can look like a solution to a problem you do not have. It is a fair objection, and it is half right. The app is the better tool for some shoppers and some baskets. The question is not whether WhatsApp beats your app. It is whether there are customers and orders your app is not reaching at all.

> Yes, a supermarket with an app should still take orders on WhatsApp, but as a parallel channel, not a replacement. The app wins for loyal customers browsing and comparing. WhatsApp wins for everyone who will never install the app, for traffic arriving from social media ads, for quick reorders and for shoppers who already know what they want. Feed both into the same order system and measure them separately.

## Why "our customers already use the app" is only half the picture

An app only counts the people who installed it. Your app's order share tells you how the customers who downloaded it behave. It says nothing about the people who saw your weekly offers on social media, wanted three things, and were never going to install an app to buy them.

That second group is not small. In Meta's [State of Business Messaging](https://whatsappbusiness.com/resources/resource-library/state-of-business-messaging/) research, a survey of 11,056 consumers across 22 markets run from April to September 2025, 73.3% said they prefer messaging when communicating with a business, and 72.4% said they are more likely to buy from a brand that offers it. Saudi Arabia and the UAE are two of the 22 markets in that survey. It is Meta's own research about its own channel, so read it as a direction rather than a forecast for your store, but it is the best public number on the question.

The useful test is in your own data: what share of your social media traffic ends in an app install, and what share of your WhatsApp support messages start with "can I order" or "do you have". If both numbers are noticeable, there are orders leaking.

## Where the app wins, and where WhatsApp wins

| Situation | Better channel | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Weekly shop by a loyal customer | App | Full catalogue, saved lists, aisle browsing, loyalty points |
| Comparing brands and sizes on a shelf | App | Product grids beat a chat for side by side comparison |
| First purchase from someone who saw an ad | WhatsApp | No install, no account, one tap from the ad |
| "Same as last week, plus milk" | WhatsApp | A sentence is faster than rebuilding a basket |
| A typed or photographed shopping list | WhatsApp | The customer already wrote the order |
| "What do I need to make pasta for six?" | WhatsApp | A question, not a search term, which a conversation handles and a search bar does not |
| A problem with an order already placed | WhatsApp | Customers already go there for this, and it is where trust is won or lost |

The pattern is simple. The app is a store you walk around. WhatsApp is the phone call to the shop where someone knows you. Most supermarkets need both, and they serve different moments.

## "Shoppers need to see products." They can, inside WhatsApp

The strongest objection to conversational grocery ordering is that people choose with their eyes. Nobody wants to describe the yoghurt they want in words. That was true of text only chat. It is not true of the WhatsApp Business Platform as documented today.

According to Meta's [developer documentation on selling products](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/whatsapp/cloud-api/guides/sell-products-and-services), checked on 6 October 2026:

- A **catalog** of your products can be connected to your WhatsApp Business account.
- A **single product message** shows one item with its image, price and description.
- A **multi-product message** shows a curated selection of up to 30 products, organised into sections.
- With ordering enabled, customers add several items to a **cart inside WhatsApp** and submit one order, with up to 99 units of each item.

So the conversation does the narrowing and the catalogue does the showing. A customer asks for olive oil, the reply shows the four oils you stock with photos and prices, and they tap the one they want. That is closer to asking a shop assistant than to scrolling an app, and it still ends with the customer choosing.

## How a WhatsApp order should reach your systems

A WhatsApp channel rarely fails because customers ignore it. It fails when it creates a second order book. An order typed into a chat, then retyped by a staff member into the real system, is slow, error prone and ends up switched off.

The setup that lasts has three parts:

1. **Identity from the phone number.** On WhatsApp the customer's number identifies them. No sign up, no password. If they also have an app account, the number links the two, so addresses and history carry across.
2. **The same order pipeline.** The WhatsApp order goes into the same order management or ERP system the app feeds, through an API, so stock, picking and delivery do not care which channel it came from. If there is no internal system to connect to, a standalone dashboard holds WhatsApp orders until there is.
3. **Separate measurement.** Tag every order with its channel. You want to know what WhatsApp brings that the app did not, not a blended number that hides it.

We covered the integration side for delivery businesses in [how to connect WhatsApp orders to fleet software](/blog/connect-whatsapp-orders-fleet-software). The principle is identical for grocery: one source of truth for orders, whatever the door.

## What a supermarket should not put on WhatsApp

Not everything belongs in a chat. Full catalogue browsing is better in the app. Loyalty scheme mechanics, account settings and long order histories are app jobs. And anything that needs a human decision, such as a refund on a damaged delivery, should be handed to a person quickly rather than handled by automation. We wrote about where that line sits for retail in [can AI actually handle retail customer service](/blog/ai-customer-service-retail).

The other limit is cost. Replies inside a conversation the customer started are free for the first 1,000 per business phone number each month on the WhatsApp Business Platform, but promotional messages you send first are charged per delivered message under Meta's [pricing rules](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/whatsapp/pricing/). A WhatsApp grocery channel works best when customers come to you, which is exactly why it pairs well with ads that open a WhatsApp chat. We go through that, and how to sell more inside each order, in [how to upsell groceries on WhatsApp](/blog/upsell-groceries-whatsapp).

## Where plumcut fits

plumcut builds and runs the conversation layer on top of a store's own catalogue, prices and offers. plum reads what the customer asks for, matches it to real products, shows options with images and prices, takes the order and sends it into the store's system, or into a standalone dashboard if there is no system to connect to yet. It runs next to the app, not instead of it. You can see the flow on [how it works](/how-it-works) and the full scope on [solutions](/solutions).

## What to do this week

Pull two numbers. First, the share of your WhatsApp support messages in the last month that were really an attempt to buy something: "do you have", "how much is", "can you deliver". Second, the click to install rate on your last social media campaign. If the first is above zero and the second is low, you have customers who want to order and a door that is too heavy for them. Start with one category, such as fresh produce or a weekly offer, on WhatsApp, routed into your existing order system, and compare it to the app for a month.

# How to Upsell Groceries on WhatsApp

Source: https://plumcut.com/blog/upsell-groceries-whatsapp
Published: 2026-10-06

To upsell groceries on WhatsApp, open the chat from a Meta ad, turn the shopper's recipe or list into a basket, and suggest only items that complete it, one at a time.

Grocery runs on thin margins and frequent repeat visits, so basket size is the number that matters. Most supermarket upselling happens on a shelf end or in an app banner, aimed at nobody in particular. A conversation is different, because the customer has just told you what they are trying to do. This guide covers both halves: getting shoppers into a WhatsApp conversation straight from an ad, and growing the basket once they are there.

> To upsell groceries on WhatsApp, start the conversation from a Meta ad that opens WhatsApp directly, let the customer state a goal ("pasta for six tonight") or paste a list, then match each item to a real product with an image and price and suggest only what completes that goal: the sauce, the cheese, the dessert, the live offer, the item that crosses the free delivery threshold. One suggestion per step. A declined offer ends it.

## Step one: send ad traffic straight into WhatsApp

The usual grocery ad sends people to an app store or a website. Every step in between, the download, the sign up, the search, loses shoppers. Meta's [ads that click to WhatsApp](https://whatsappbusiness.com/products/create-ads-that-click-to-whatsapp/) remove those steps: the person taps the ad and a WhatsApp chat with your business opens. In Meta Ads Manager you build the ad as usual and, at the destination step, choose messaging apps and then WhatsApp.

Three things make this especially suited to grocery:

- **No account.** The shopper's phone number identifies them. There is nothing to install or register before the first order.
- **The ad can start the conversation.** The ad's message template in Ads Manager can set a pre-filled first message, which the shopper can edit before sending, as described in [Braze's documentation of the format](https://www.braze.com/docs/user_guide/channels/whatsapp/use_cases/ads_that_click_to_whatsapp/). A tap on a "Weekend barbecue box" ad lands the shopper in a chat that already knows what they came for.
- **The first days are free to message.** Under Meta's [WhatsApp pricing rules](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/whatsapp/pricing), checked on 11 October 2026, when a customer messages you through a Click to WhatsApp ad on the WhatsApp Android or iOS app and you reply within the customer service window, your first reply opens a free entry point window that can stay open for up to 7 days. During it, marketing, utility, authentication and service messages, templates included, are not charged, though Meta Business Agent messages still are. For a grocer that covers the order, the confirmation, the delivery update and a follow up about the next shop.

That last point matters for the economics. Outside that window, promotional messages you send first are marketing templates, charged per delivered message. We broke down the full structure in [what the WhatsApp Business API really costs](/blog/whatsapp-business-api-cost).

## Step two: let the customer state a goal, not a search term

A search bar needs a product name. A conversation accepts a goal. That is the whole advantage, and it is where the upsell starts.

Three kinds of message a grocer can expect, and what each one opens up:

| The customer writes | What it tells you | The natural addition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "I want to make pasta for six tonight" | A complete meal, a quantity and a deadline | Sauce, parmesan, garlic bread, a dessert |
| A pasted or photographed shopping list | The core basket, already decided | Items usually bought with those, offers on listed brands |
| "Same as last week" | A repeat basket | What changed since: a new offer, a seasonal item |

Regional shoppers rarely write in textbook English. A message like "bade 2 kilo banadoura w khebez" mixes Arabizi with a quantity and a product. A conversation layer that only understands clean English product names misses that order entirely. We covered how far Arabic and Arabizi understanding has come in [whether AI customer service really works in Arabic](/blog/ai-customer-service-arabic).

## Step three: match every item to a real product, with a picture

The goal becomes a basket only when every ingredient maps to something on your shelves, at today's price. This is the part that needs your catalogue, not a generic chatbot.

WhatsApp now supports this visually. According to Meta's [developer documentation on selling products](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/whatsapp/cloud-api/guides/sell-products-and-services), a business can connect a product catalog to its WhatsApp account, send single product messages with an image, price and description, and send multi-product messages showing up to 30 products in sections. Customers add items to a cart inside WhatsApp and submit one order.

So when "pasta" matches five pastas, the shopper is shown the five with photos and prices and taps one. When a brand is out of stock, the substitute is offered with its picture rather than silently swapped. Substitution handled well is itself a sale saved.

## Step four: suggest what completes the basket, once

Here is a worked example. It is illustrative, not a customer conversation.

A shopper taps a weekend recipe ad and writes that they want to make pasta for six tonight. The reply confirms quantities and shows two pastas and three sauces with prices. The shopper picks one of each. The next message adds one suggestion: parmesan, with the reason attached, because the recipe calls for it and it is on offer this week. The shopper adds it. Before confirming, the reply notes that the basket is a small amount short of free delivery and names one relevant item that would cross the line. The shopper declines. The order is confirmed with no further offers.

Four rules sit behind that exchange:

1. **Only suggest what completes the stated goal.** Parmesan for pasta, charcoal for a barbecue, lemons for fish. Not this week's random promotion.
2. **Attach the reason.** "It is in the recipe and 20% off this week" sells. "You may also like" does not.
3. **Use the offers you already run.** The conversation is a new place to put the promotions your team already sets, matched to baskets they actually fit.
4. **One suggestion per step, and a no ends it.** We went through why in detail in [how to upsell and cross-sell inside a conversation](/blog/upsell-cross-sell-in-conversation).

## Step five: read what customers ask for

Every conversation records something an app search log never captures: what people were trying to cook, which items they asked for that you do not stock, which substitutes they refused. Across thousands of conversations that is a demand signal for buying and promotions. It is also the part most grocers never see, because the conversations live on staff phones.

## Where plumcut fits

plumcut builds and runs this conversation layer on top of a store's own catalogue, prices and offers. plum takes the shopper from the ad into the chat, turns a goal or a list into a matched basket with images and prices, suggests what completes it, takes the order into the store's system, and shows the owner what customers actually asked for. It works next to the store's app, not instead of it, a point we covered in [WhatsApp ordering for supermarkets](/blog/whatsapp-ordering-supermarkets). See the flow on [how it works](/how-it-works).

## What to do this week

Pick one meal your customers already buy for, a weekend barbecue, a family pasta night, a Friday breakfast. Write down the eight to twelve products that make it up and which of them are on offer. Then run one small Click to WhatsApp ad for that meal and answer every chat by hand for a week, logging what people ask for and what they add when you suggest the missing item. That week tells you whether the channel is worth automating, using your own customers rather than anyone's averages.

# AI Customer Service Cost in 2026: The Hidden Fees

Source: https://plumcut.com/blog/ai-customer-service-hidden-costs
Published: 2026-10-03

AI customer service costs about 10 to 280 US dollars a month on the advertised plan, based on 12 vendor pages checked on 3 October 2026. The real bill adds 0.90 to 2.00 dollars per automated resolution, plus seats, contact overages and Meta's WhatsApp fees.

You found a tool that says 29 dollars a month. Then the first invoice arrived and it said something else. That gap is not a scam, it is how the category prices: the plan is the entry ticket, and the automation, the people, the contacts and the WhatsApp messages are each metered on their own line.

> AI customer service usually costs far more than its headline plan. On 12 vendor pages checked on 3 October 2026, the advertised plan ran from about 10 to 280 US dollars a month, but the AI itself was often billed separately, at 0.90 to 2.00 US dollars per automated conversation or resolution. On top of that come seats, contact or ticket overages, and Meta's WhatsApp template fees, which vary by country. To compare vendors honestly, add every line for your real monthly volume. plumcut takes the other route: a one time setup fee, then a fixed monthly fee in wide bands with a ceiling, with Meta and AI usage passed through at cost.

## The six lines behind every AI customer service bill

Almost every invoice in this category is built from the same six parts. Vendors differ in which ones they show on the pricing page.

| Line | What it charges for | Where you will see it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Plan or seat | Access, usually per person who logs in | Every helpdesk |
| 2. Automation | Each conversation or resolution the AI closes | Intercom, Zendesk, Gorgias, Tidio, Interakt |
| 3. Overage | Tickets or monthly active contacts above the plan limit | Gorgias, respond.io, SleekFlow |
| 4. Meta's message fees | WhatsApp template messages, priced by country | Everyone on WhatsApp, passed through |
| 5. Provider fees on messages or numbers | A per message fee, a licence or a number hosting fee | Twilio, 360dialog, SleekFlow |
| 6. Your team's time | Building flows, writing answers, fixing what breaks | Never on the invoice |

The sixth line is the one that decides whether a cheap tool stays cheap. A self serve platform at 50 dollars a month that needs a person half a day a week to maintain it is not a 50 dollar product.

## What 12 vendors actually charge, checked on 3 October 2026

plumcut sells in this category, so this is a comparison written by a participant. Every figure below comes from the vendor's own pricing or documentation page on 3 October 2026, follows the same six lines, and links to the page so you can check it. Prices change. Pull the current number before you budget; the structure is the part that lasts. Where a page did not state something, the table says not stated.

| Vendor | Headline plan | The lines that are not in the headline |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Intercom](https://www.intercom.com/pricing) | Essential 29 US dollars per seat a month, billed annually | Fin AI at 0.99 US dollars per outcome, on top of seats |
| [Zendesk](https://www.zendesk.com/pricing/) | Support Team 19 US dollars per agent a month, paid yearly | 5 automated resolutions per agent a month included on Team plans, then 1.50 US dollars each committed or 2.00 pay as you go |
| [Gorgias](https://www.gorgias.com/pricing) | Starter 10 US dollars a month with 50 tickets | 0.40 US dollars per ticket over the limit, its AI at 0.90 US dollars per automated interaction on annual or 1.00 on monthly |
| [Tidio](https://www.tidio.com/pricing/) | Starter 24.17 US dollars a month for 100 billable conversations, billed annually | Lyro AI sold separately, from 32.50 US dollars a month for 50 AI conversations |
| [respond.io](https://respond.io/pricing) | Starter 79 US dollars a month, billed annually | 12 US dollars per 100 extra monthly active contacts on Growth, 15 on Advanced; WhatsApp fees not included |
| [Wati](https://www.wati.io/pricing/) | Plan prices load dynamically and were not captured on 3 October 2026, check the page | Extra users at 24 US dollars a month on Pro, 69 on Business; per message charges for marketing, utility and authentication; Shopify integration 4.99 US dollars a month |
| [SleekFlow](https://sleekflow.io/pricing) | Pro 109 US dollars a month, billed yearly, with 500 monthly active contacts | WhatsApp number hosting at 15 US dollars a month; conversation rates per SleekFlow's own rate card |
| [Interakt](https://www.interakt.shop/pricing/) | Growth 55 US dollars a month plus taxes | AI add-on at 74.99 US dollars with 100 AI messages, then 0.011 US dollars per AI message |
| [Twilio](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/whatsapp/pricing) | No platform plan, pay per message | 0.005 US dollars per WhatsApp message inbound or outbound, plus Meta's template fee passed through |
| [360dialog](https://360dialog.com/pricing) | 49 euros per number a month plus Meta fees | States no markup on Meta fees; higher tiers at 99 and 500 euros |
| [Meta](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/whatsapp/pricing) | Per template message since 1 July 2025 | Rate set by template category and the recipient's country code |
| [plumcut](/pricing) | One time setup fee, then a fixed monthly fee set by what the solution does | Meta messaging and AI model usage billed at cost with no margin; fee steps up in wide bands to a ceiling |

Three patterns stand out once the lines sit side by side.

**The AI is usually a second product.** Intercom, Zendesk, Gorgias, Tidio and Interakt all price the automation separately from the plan. The plan buys you an inbox. The thing you came for is metered.

**Contacts are a growth tax.** respond.io and SleekFlow bill by monthly active contacts. Talk to more customers, which is the goal, and the bill climbs with you.

**Message fees hide in the plumbing.** Twilio's half cent per message looks small until you multiply it by every inbound and outbound message in a month. 360dialog is the opposite case: it states no markup on Meta's fees and charges a flat licence instead. Ask every provider which of those two models it follows.

## Meta's fees, and why your market matters

Meta moved WhatsApp to [per message pricing](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/whatsapp/pricing) on 1 July 2025. Since 1 October 2026 its documentation says service replies inside the customer service window are free only for the first 1,000 per business phone number each month, and utility templates are charged even inside an open window. What you pay for are template messages, marketing, utility and authentication, plus service replies past the free tier.

The rate depends on the recipient's country calling code, and the region is split in a way that matters for anyone selling across it. Saudi Arabia (966) and the United Arab Emirates (971) are listed as their own markets. Lebanon (961) sits in a grouping called Rest of Middle East. A brand messaging customers in Beirut, Riyadh and Dubai is paying three different rate lines, and a vendor quote that uses one blended number is guessing. We broke the categories down in [what the WhatsApp Business API really costs](/blog/whatsapp-business-api-cost).

## The same store, priced three ways

An illustrative calculation, not a customer result. A store with two people on the inbox and 600 conversations a month that the AI closes on its own. Annual billing prices from the table above. Meta fees left out because they are the same everywhere.

| Vendor | Seats | Automation | Overage | Monthly total before Meta fees |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Intercom, Advanced at 85 per seat | 170 | 600 × 0.99 = 594 | none | about 764 US dollars |
| Zendesk, Suite Team at 55 per agent | 110 | 10 included, 590 × 1.50 = 885 | none | about 995 US dollars |
| Gorgias, Basic at 50 with 300 tickets | 50 | 600 × 0.90 = 540 | 1,500 tickets means 1,200 × 0.40 = 480 | about 1,070 US dollars |

Now double the traffic, which is what a good season does. Every one of those totals rises, because three of the six lines are metered. That is the real cost question: not what you pay this month, but what your bill does when you succeed. We compared that effect across ten platforms in [AI customer service for retail](/blog/ai-customer-service-retail).

## Why plumcut prices the opposite way

plumcut does not sell you an inbox and a meter. It builds plum, the AI that answers, sells and books on your WhatsApp, connects it to your store and systems, and runs it for you. The [pricing](/pricing) follows from that.

- **One setup fee, stated up front.** It pays for learning your brand, building plum around your products and policies, testing it on real questions and launching. It is live in about two weeks.
- **One fixed monthly fee.** Set by what your solution does, not by how many conversations it handles. It steps up in wide bands as traffic settles higher, the top band is a ceiling, and you are told before a band changes.
- **Meta and AI usage at cost.** The two costs that genuinely scale with volume are billed to you at cost with no margin added. No per message fee on top, no per resolution charge, no contact tax.
- **No line six.** There is nobody on your side writing flows or fixing answers. That work is the service.
- **Arabic and English, built in.** No add-on for the language most of your customers write in.

Line by line, that removes the seat charge, the automation meter, the overage and the hidden staff time, and leaves you two numbers: a fixed fee and Meta's own rates.

## When a metered tool is the better buy

Plainly, because a comparison that never says this is an advert. If your volume is very low or very uneven, a per resolution tool like Gorgias or Intercom can cost less than any fixed fee, since a quiet month costs almost nothing. If you already run a trained support team on Zendesk, adding its automation is less disruptive than switching. And if you want to build and own every flow yourself, a self serve platform like respond.io or Wati is the right shape. If none of those describes you, and you would rather have one predictable number and nobody on your team maintaining a bot, [see how plumcut works](/how-it-works).

## What to do this week

1. Pull last month's numbers: conversations, people on the inbox, unique customers who messaged, and how many template messages you sent per country.
2. For each vendor you are considering, fill in all six lines from the table, not just line one.
3. Run the same sum at double your volume. The vendor whose total moves least is the one built for a growing brand.
4. Then ask plum for a fixed quote and compare it with the six line total, not with the headline plan.

# AI Chatbot vs Hiring Customer Service in Lebanon and GCC

Source: https://plumcut.com/blog/ai-chatbot-vs-hiring-customer-service
Published: 2026-10-03

An AI chatbot is cheaper than hiring customer service staff in Lebanon and GCC markets such as Saudi Arabia and the UAE when questions repeat, since one hire covers 48 of 168 weekly hours.

Messages are piling up, replies are going out late, and the obvious fix is to hire someone. Before you post the job ad, run the numbers properly, because the cost of a customer service hire is not the salary on the offer letter, and one hire does not cover the hours your customers are actually messaging.

> For repetitive customer questions, an AI chatbot is almost always cheaper than hiring. A week has 168 hours, and the labour laws of Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Lebanon cap a standard working week at 48 hours, so keeping one seat filled around the clock takes about three and a half people before anyone takes leave. Each hire then adds employer costs: social insurance, an end of service payment, paid leave and recruitment. An AI like plum answers at every hour for one fixed monthly fee. Hiring still wins for judgment work, refunds, exceptions and complaints, which is why the best answer is usually AI for the volume and people for the decisions.

## The number most people get wrong: coverage

Your customers do not message in office hours. They message after dinner, on Friday, during Ramadan nights. A hire covers their shift and nothing else.

| Country | Standard maximum working week | Hires needed to cover 168 hours | Paid annual leave on top |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Saudi Arabia | [48 hours](https://www.hrsd.gov.sa/en/knowledge-centre/articles/312), 36 in Ramadan for Muslim employees | 3.5, or 4.7 in Ramadan | [At least 21 days](https://www.hrsd.gov.sa/en/knowledge-centre/articles/321), 30 after five years |
| UAE | [8 hours a day or 48 a week](https://u.ae/en/information-and-services/jobs/Sector-of-employment/employment-in-the-private-sector/working-hours) | 3.5 | 30 days after one year of service |
| Lebanon | [48 hours](https://www.nrc.no/globalassets/pdf/guidelines/guide-to-employment-rights/lebanon-employment-rights-guide---english.pdf) under the Labour Code | 3.5 | 15 days after one year |

So the honest comparison is never "one salary against one subscription". It is either three and a half salaries against one subscription, or one salary plus a promise to customers that nobody answers after six. Most brands quietly choose the second, and pay for it in carts that go cold overnight. We looked at what that silence costs in [what happens when your store gets more messages than your team can read](/blog/too-many-customer-messages-retail).

## What a hire costs beyond the salary

Every country in the region adds employer costs that never appear on the offer letter. Checked on official or published legal sources on 3 October 2026; this is a guide, not payroll advice.

**Saudi Arabia.** For a Saudi employee, the employer pays GOSI [annuities at 9 percent](https://www.gosi.gov.sa/GOSIOnline/FAQ_Employer?locale=en_US) for existing contributors, and GOSI's own guidance says the rate for new entrants under the new Social Insurance Law rises in half point steps to 11 percent. On top of that, [2 percent for occupational hazards](https://www.gosi.gov.sa/GOSIOnline/FAQ_Employer?locale=en_US), which also applies to non-Saudi employees, and [0.75 percent for SANED](https://www.gosi.gov.sa/GOSIOnline/FAQ_Unemployment_Insurance_(SANED)?locale=en_US) unemployment insurance. The [Labor Law](https://www.hrsd.gov.sa/sites/default/files/2023-02/Labor.pdf) adds an end of service award of half a month's wage for each of the first five years and a full month for each year after.

**United Arab Emirates.** The [end of service gratuity](https://u.ae/en/information-and-services/jobs/Sector-of-employment/employment-in-the-private-sector/end-of-service-benefits-for-employees-in-the-private-sector) is 21 days of salary for each of the first five years and 30 days for each year after, capped at two years of wages. If you hire an Emirati, the private sector [minimum wage is AED 6,000 a month](https://u.ae/en/information-and-services/jobs/Sector-of-employment/employment-in-the-private-sector/emiratis-employment-in-private-sector) from 1 January 2026.

**Lebanon.** A published legal guide to Lebanese employment rights lists employer NSSF contributions of 8.5 percent for end of service indemnity, 6 percent for family allowances and 8 percent for sickness and maternity, about 22.5 percent in total before wage ceilings. The private sector minimum wage was [raised to LBP 28 million a month](https://wageindicator.org/work/minimum-wage/updates/2025/minimum-wage-updated-in-lebanon-from-01-august-2025-august-08-2025/) in mid 2025.

Then add what no law lists: recruiting, the weeks of training before a new hire answers confidently, a manager's time, a laptop and a phone line, and starting over when they leave.

## Run it for your own store

An illustrative method, not a measured result. Plug in your own salary figure; we are deliberately not quoting market salaries, because they vary too much by city and seniority to be useful.

1. **Monthly salary** of one customer service hire: call it S.
2. **Employer on-costs**: in Lebanon, roughly 22.5 percent NSSF from the guide above. In Saudi Arabia, for a Saudi hire, about 11.75 percent rising toward 13.75 percent with GOSI, plus the end of service accrual. In the UAE, the gratuity alone accrues at 21 days of salary for every year of the first five.
3. **Coverage**: multiply by 3.5 if you want every hour covered, or accept that one hire means one shift.
4. **Hidden overhead**: recruitment, training and management time, honestly estimated.

A single Lebanese hire on salary S therefore costs about 1.225 S a month before overhead, and round the clock cover costs about 4.3 S. Compare that with a fixed monthly AI fee plus Meta's own message charges, and the gap is usually not close. To price the AI side properly, line by line, see [what AI customer service really costs](/blog/ai-customer-service-hidden-costs).

## What an AI does better, and what a person does better

| Job | AI on WhatsApp | A trained person |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Is this in stock, how much, do you deliver to my area" | Instant, at any hour, from live data | Accurate, but only in their shift |
| The same question for the hundredth time today | Same quality the hundredth time | Quality drops by evening |
| Arabic, English and Arabizi in one chat | Handles all three when built for it | Depends on the hire |
| A sudden flood of messages after a campaign | Answers them all at once | Queue forms |
| Refunds, exceptions, goodwill | Should hand over | Should decide |
| An angry customer you let down | Should hand over, fast | The right person for it |

Meta's [WhatsApp Business messaging policy](https://whatsappbusiness.com/policy/) allows automated replies in the 24 hour customer service window but requires prompt, clear and direct escalation to a person. So the realistic design is not AI instead of people. It is AI for the volume and your existing team for the moments that need judgment, which usually means you do not need the extra hire at all.

## Why plumcut is built for exactly this decision

Most AI tools hand you software and leave the work of running it to you, which quietly brings the hire back: somebody has to write the flows, update the answers and fix what breaks. plumcut removes that too.

- **Done for you.** plumcut learns your brand, builds plum around your products, prices and policies, connects it to your store, and [runs and improves it](/how-it-works). Nobody on your team operates a tool.
- **Every hour, every message.** plum answers, sells and books on your WhatsApp at 3 a.m. and on a Friday afternoon, in Arabic and English.
- **Hands over at the right moment.** Tricky and sensitive conversations go to your team with the context attached, so the people you have spend their time on decisions, not on copy and paste.
- **One fixed number.** A one time setup fee, then a [fixed monthly fee](/pricing) in wide bands with a ceiling, and Meta and AI usage at cost. No gratuity, no social insurance, no leave cover, no notice period.
- **Live in about two weeks.**

There are cases where hiring is the better first move. If your messages are mostly unique judgment calls rather than repeated questions, or you are still agreeing internally on what the right answers are, a person will serve you better today, and we wrote the case for waiting in [when your business is ready for AI customer service](/blog/when-ready-for-ai-customer-service). For everyone else drowning in the same questions, the cheaper hire is not a person.

## What to do this week

1. Count the messages that arrived outside working hours in the last two weeks, and how long each waited.
2. Write down the fully loaded monthly cost of the hire you are considering, using the steps above, not the salary.
3. Mark last week's questions as repeatable or judgment. The repeatable share is what an AI takes off the new hire's desk.
4. Ask plum for a fixed monthly quote and put it next to the number from step 2.
